```{r}
#| label: setup
REPO <- "https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/bsz-analysis/"
SA <- normalizePath("..")
link <- function(path, text = path) sprintf('<a href="%s%s"><code>%s</code></a>', REPO, path, text)
show <- function(df) knitr::kable(df, format = "html", escape = FALSE,
                                  table.attr = 'class="table table-sm"')
first_comment <- function(f) {
  l <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE, n = 12)
  l <- sub("^#+ ?", "", l[grepl("^#", l)])
  l <- l[nzchar(trimws(l))]
  if (length(l)) l[1] else ""
}
tests <- read.csv("data/test-results.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

::: {.report-intro}
![](assets/opa/opa-materials.png){.opa-figure}

This page is a guide to the **Open Materials** layer (the repository) of the BSZ analysis (Boll, Saez and Zucman, BSZ, plus the
Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske (GGSS) expert report): what to download, what
to run, and what the checks found. Everything lives in one repository,
[fhoces/opa-prop40](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40), under `bsz-analysis/`.
The tables on this page are built from the files themselves when the page is rendered, so
they cannot fall out of date with the code without a re-render showing it.
:::

## Rebuild everything

```sh
git clone https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40 && cd opa-prop40/bsz-analysis
curl -L -o original-materials/BSZ_MainTablesFigures.xlsx \
     https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/BSZ_MainTablesFigures.xlsx   # check the SHA-256 below
Rscript -e 'targets::tar_make(names = !tidyselect::any_of(c("report_html","report_pdf")))'
Rscript tools/site-test-results.R        # the full test suite; writes site/data/test-results.csv
cd site && quarto render repro.qmd && quarto render materials.qmd
cd slides && Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("slides.Rmd")'
```

The pipeline is an R [`{targets}`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) project (an R package
that runs the pipeline's steps in order and records which outputs are current). The
default workbook vintage (the dated version of the workbook a number comes from) is August
2026; `BSZ_VINTAGE=may` switches every
vintage-dependent path, column and constant to May. `CAWTBSZ_MATERIALS` points the
pipeline at the sources if they are not in `original-materials/`.

Every computation also has a Python twin in `r link("py/")`, with the same function names
as in `R/`. After `pip install -r requirements.txt`, the command `python py/run_export.py`
(about 2 seconds) writes the same results to `export/py/`, and
`r link("tests/testthat/test-py-parity.R")` checks each file against R's. The report's
code folds show both languages.

## Tests

```{r}
#| label: tests
by_file <- aggregate(cbind(blocks = 1, passed, failed, skipped) ~ file, data = tests, FUN = sum)
by_file$file <- vapply(by_file$file, function(f) link(paste0("tests/testthat/", f), f), "")
show(rbind(by_file, data.frame(file = "<b>total</b>", blocks = sum(by_file$blocks),
                               passed = sum(by_file$passed), failed = sum(by_file$failed),
                               skipped = sum(by_file$skipped))))
```

Last run: `r tests$run_date[1]`, `r tools::toTitleCase(tests$vintage[1])` vintage: **`r sum(tests$passed)`
expectations passed, `r sum(tests$failed)` failed**, in `r nrow(tests)` test blocks. Of
these, `r sum(tests$passed[tests$file != "test-site.R"])` belong to the reproduction itself
and `r sum(tests$passed[tests$file == "test-site.R"])` to this site: they check that the
explorer reproduces Table 5 to 1e-12, that `explorer/grid.js` is the exporter's own output,
and that every number typed into a hand-written page still matches the pipeline. GitHub
Actions rebuilds the pipeline and runs the suite on every push that touches
`bsz-analysis/` (`.github/workflows/bsz-ci.yml`); it does not render the Quarto pages or
the slides.

## Scripts

```{r}
#| label: scripts
# One-line roles, from the repository README's layout section. A file not in
# this list falls back to its own first comment line, so a new script still
# shows up here.
role <- c(
  "ingest_excel.R" = "reads the workbook: sheet reader, vintage switch, source directory",
  "excel_cells.R" = "single-cell and row/column readers shared by the compute files",
  "vintage.R" = "everything that differs between the May and August workbooks, in one place",
  "data_sheets.R" = "14 extractors, one per workbook sheet the pipeline reads",
  "compute_data_sec_agg.R" = "yearly totals from the billionaire list (drops the duplicated rows)",
  "compute_pareto.R" = "Pareto extrapolation of missing billionaires; the Laffer curve",
  "compute_tab5.R" = "Table 5: the estimating function the explorer also runs, and the four estimate rows of the one-time tax",
  "compute_billionaires_ca_inctax.R" = "CA income tax of all billionaires (FTB + Pareto), and all taxes",
  "compute_shortrunseries.R" = "wealth growth panel and the 2025 snapshot",
  "compute_top4taxes.R" = "taxes of the top 4 by year, 2004-2025",
  "tables.R" = "the six gt tables",
  "figures.R" = "the twelve ggplot figures",
  "render.R" = "writes tables and figures to outputs/",
  "verify.R" = "the test helper that compares R with the workbook's cached cells",
  "code_listing.R" = "helper for code listings in the original report",
  "site_exports.R" = "this site's data: the dials, the grid (computed by compute_tab5.R), input origins")
fs <- sort(list.files(file.path(SA, "R"), pattern = "[.]R$"))
show(data.frame(
  file = vapply(fs, function(f) link(paste0("R/", f)), ""),
  lines = vapply(fs, function(f) length(readLines(file.path(SA, "R", f), warn = FALSE)), 1L),
  `what it does` = vapply(fs, function(f) if (!is.na(role[f])) role[[f]] else first_comment(file.path(SA, "R", f)), ""),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL))
```

Also: `r link("_targets.R")` (the pipeline: which function builds which result),
`r link("tools/site-test-results.R")` (runs the suite for this page), and the site sources
`r link("site/repro.qmd")`, `r link("site/materials.qmd")`, `r link("site/slides/slides.Rmd")`,
`r link("site/index.html")` and `r link("site/explorer/index.html")`.

## Data files the site publishes

```{r}
#| label: data
desc <- c(
  "grid.csv" = "every cell of the explorer: six inputs and seven outcomes",
  "inputs.csv" = "every input of the one-time estimate, with value, origin label and source",
  "tab5.csv" = "Table 5, the four estimate rows, as the pipeline computes them",
  "tab5-vs-printed.csv" = "every Table 5 cell against the digit printed in the paper",
  "leavers.csv" = "the seven named leavers of Table 5 rows 3 and 4",
  "test-results.csv" = "one row per test block from the last full run")
dfs <- names(desc)
show(data.frame(
  file = sprintf('<a href="data/%s"><code>%s</code></a>', dfs, dfs),
  rows = vapply(dfs, function(f) nrow(read.csv(file.path("data", f))), 1L),
  columns = vapply(dfs, function(f) ncol(read.csv(file.path("data", f))), 1L),
  contents = unname(desc), row.names = NULL))
```

Every file except `test-results.csv` is written by a target in `_targets.R`
(`site_grid_csv`, `site_inputs_csv`, `site_tab5_csv`, `site_tab5_printed_csv`,
`site_leavers_csv`; the explorer's
`grid.js` by `site_grid_js`). None is edited by hand.

## Sources

The authors' workbook and paper are not redistributed here. The manifest records where each
file came from, its SHA-256 and its terms:

```{r}
#| label: sources
ds <- read.csv(file.path(SA, "DATA-SOURCES.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show(data.frame(
  file = sprintf("<code>%s</code>", sub("^original-materials/", "", ds$file)),
  provider = ds$provider,
  obtained = paste(ds$obtained_via, ds$date_obtained),
  `SHA-256 (first 12)` = sprintf("<code>%s</code>", substr(ds$sha256, 1, 12)),
  terms = ds$terms,
  check.names = FALSE))
```

Full rows, including what each source feeds: `r link("DATA-SOURCES.csv")`; the column
definitions: `r link("DATA-SOURCES.md")`. The author-shared bundle is confidential. The SQL in
`sql/` rebuilds the workbook's data sheets from it and checks them against the public workbook;
only that comparison is reported, and none of the bundle's contents is committed or shown.

## What the checks found

```{r}
#| label: notes-numbers
# The figures in the notes below, computed from the workbook when the page is rendered.
invisible(lapply(list.files(file.path(SA, "R"), pattern = "[.]R$", full.names = TRUE), source))
n_inp <- tab5_scoring_inputs(compute_pareto_missing(extract_pareto_missing()),
                             extract_tab2(), extract_tab3())
n_t5  <- compute_tab5(compute_pareto_missing(extract_pareto_missing()), extract_tab2(), extract_tab3())
n_pr  <- compare_tab5_printed(n_t5)
n_miss <- n_pr[!n_pr$matches_printed, ]
stopifnot(nrow(n_miss) == 2, all(abs(trunc(n_miss$reproduced * 100) / 100 - n_miss$printed) < 1e-9))
n_may2 <- withr::with_envvar(c(BSZ_VINTAGE = "may"), {
  mi <- tab5_scoring_inputs(compute_pareto_missing(extract_pareto_missing()), extract_tab2(), extract_tab3())
  score_tab5_cell(mi, pareto = TRUE)[["annual_ca_inctax_loss"]]
})
n_ratio <- n_inp$C / n_inp$W0                   # Table 5's income tax per dollar of wealth
n_years <- 0.05 / n_ratio                        # years for the lost income tax to equal the tax
n_laf   <- compute_fig8_laffer()
n_peak  <- optimize(function(t) t * exp(-10 * t) * (1 - t)^15, c(0, 0.2), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
n_kept  <- (n_laf$actual_tax_revenue[which.min(abs(n_laf$tax_rate - 0.012))] - 0.002 * 2000) / (0.01 * 2000)
n_d15   <- 1 - 0.99^15
b3 <- function(x) sprintf("\\$%.3fB", abs(x))
p1 <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
```

The code reproduces the paper's published results from the authors' public workbook: Table 5,
the other tables and figures it builds, every variation of Table 5 the paper prints, and the
other numbers checked on the [checks page](checks.html). A figure counts as reproduced when it
rounds to the printed digit, or when the paper prints the same value cut rather than rounded.
A figure the text derives counts as reproduced when the inputs the text states give it.

The eight notes below are kept for transparency. Each records a place where the paper's text,
its tables and the workbook describe a step differently. None is a failure to reproduce a
printed result. They are of three kinds, and each note states its kind:

- **Rounding** (note 1): the paper prints a value at a different rounding from its workbook.
- **Small numerical difference** (notes 7 and 8): the text uses a first-order formula, and the
  workbook's exact curve gives a slightly different figure. Each note gives the size.
- **Documentation** (notes 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6): the text, a table label and the workbook describe
  one calculation differently, or use different inputs for it. Each printed result reproduces
  from the inputs stated beside it.

An earlier version of these pages called the first note a pair of cells that "differ from the
workbook", the repeated rows "a data-entry error", and notes 6 to 8 numbers that "differ" or are
"close". They were reclassified on 2026-10-16 under the standard first applied to the
[JR analysis](../../rjkdc-analysis/site/materials.html#reproduction-notes);
`feedback/007-2026-10-16-bsz-reproduction-standard/REPORT.md` gives each item's old and new label.

### Notes on the authors' materials

1. **Rounding.** Table 5 prints the income tax loss of rows 2 and 3 as
   \$`r sprintf("%.2f", -n_miss$printed[1])`B and \$`r sprintf("%.2f", -n_miss$printed[2])`B a year. The
   workbook, and this code, give `r b3(n_miss$reproduced[1])` and `r b3(n_miss$reproduced[2])`,
   which round to \$`r sprintf("%.2f", -round(n_miss$reproduced[1], 2))`B and
   \$`r sprintf("%.2f", -round(n_miss$reproduced[2], 2))`B. Both printed figures are the workbook's value
   cut at the second decimal rather than rounded, one unit lower in the last digit
   (`r b3(n_miss$reproduced[1] - n_miss$printed[1])` and `r b3(n_miss$reproduced[2] - n_miss$printed[2])` a
   year). Row 2's printed figure is also what the May version printed, from `r b3(n_may2)` in the May
   workbook. No
   other printed number is built on these two cells. A test checks both.
2. **Documentation.** The workbook's year-by-year list of billionaires (`data_sec_all`) repeats
   rows 1338 to 1341, four 2025 entries, at rows 1342 to 1345. Counting both copies gives 244
   billionaires for 2025. The workbook's own aggregate sheet and the paper's text give 240, and
   so does the pipeline, which drops the repeat (`r link("R/compute_data_sec_agg.R")`). No
   printed number changes.
3. **Documentation.** `Tab5!H6` types the share of income tax lost to leavers as a literal 0.05.
   The row label, "10% evasion/avoidance (half due to mobility)", describes it as avoidance times
   the share due to mobility, 0.10 &times; 0.5, the same value. The [explorer](explorer/) uses the
   product, so the share moves with those two dials. At the authors' values the results are
   identical.
4. **Documentation.** Table 5's row 4 is described as rows 2 and 3 together, but it does not
   subtract the phase-in deduction that row 2 subtracts (`Tab5!F9` against `Tab5!F7`). The printed
   \$`r round(n_t5$wealth_tax_revenue[4])` billion comes from the workbook as it is, and this
   reproduction and the explorer follow it. A consistent treatment would give
   \$`r sprintf("%.1f", n_t5$wealth_tax_revenue[4] - n_inp$row4_phasein_gap)` billion,
   \$`r sprintf("%.1f", n_inp$row4_phasein_gap)` billion less.
5. **Documentation.** Appendix Table A1's annualized growth row (`TabA1!B18:G18`) spreads the
   growth from 1982 to 2026 over 43 years. Table 1 uses 44 (`Tab1!C18:H18`). The paper prints the
   workbook's 43-year values, and so does this reproduction. The
   [report](repro.html#appendix-table-a1-us-billionaires) states what 44 would give.
6. **Documentation.** The text's break-even (PDF p.22: 25 years if all billionaires left, 100 if
   one fourth did) uses the ratio of income tax to wealth the text states, about 0.2% a year
   (the abstract and Table 2's recent years). Both figures reproduce from that ratio. Table 5 uses
   the 2019-2025 average tax against 1 July 2026 wealth, `r p1(n_ratio, 2)`. On Table 5's inputs
   the break-even is about `r round(n_years)` years (`r round(4 * n_years)` if one fourth left).
7. **Small numerical difference.** The text gives the revenue-maximising rate of a permanent
   tax with de-concentration as 1/(1 + d + e) = 1/26 = 3.8% (PDF p.30), a first-order formula.
   The exact peak of the workbook's own Figure 9 curve, which this code reproduces, is
   `r p1(n_peak)`. In the same way, the text's "about 15%" of the base lost at a 1% tax is
   d &times; 1%. The curve's factor, 1 &minus; 0.99<sup>15</sup>, gives `r p1(n_d15)`.
8. **Small numerical difference.** The text says a 1% permanent tax keeps 88% of its mechanical
   revenue (PDF pp.29-30), adding up first-order effects (100% &minus; 10% &minus; 2%). The
   workbook's curve gives `r p1(n_kept)`.

### Errors in this OPA, found and fixed

- **A display error** in this reproduction's Tables 1 and A1: the display put Panel B's values
  under Panel A's headers and formats and kept the May workbook's labels (GDP for AGI, 2025 for
  2026); fixed in the display code on 2026-10-15.
- **Appendix Table A1 at first used 44 years**, so three cells of the annualized row printed
  lower than the paper. It now uses 43, as the paper and the workbook do (note 5), and a test
  checks each cell of the row.
- **A malformed row in our own source manifest**: two `provider` fields contained an
  unquoted comma, which shifted every later column for any CSV reader; quoted on 2026-09-23.
- **Stale positions in this OPA's code.** When the authors updated the workbook, 184 of this
  reproduction's tests failed on row positions and constants that this OPA's code had fixed at
  the earlier layout. All were fixed (`r link("VERIFY-AUGUST.md")`).

### Not reproduced

The paper's Figure 8 and Appendix Figure A1 (wealth relative to AGI) have no builder yet. The raw
data behind the workbook is taken as given.
